title: Tariff Fatigue And Trump’s Next Move
text:
Tariff Fatigue And Trump’s Next Move

Tom Miller

Gavekal Research | 27 Nov 2026

Financial markets may have succumbed to Trump tariff fatigue, but America’s trading partners cannot afford to. While markets barely flinched at Wednesday’s announcement of proposed new Section 301 tariffs on 14 trading partners, China and Brazil both raised the prospect of retaliation. The muted market reaction is understandable: tariffs are largely baked into investors’ calculations and the proposed increases for most trading partners are modest. Goldman Sachs estimates that the proposals would raise the overall US tariff rate from 7.8% to 9.2%. But the White House sees the tariffs as leverage to extract further concessions from China, Vietnam and India in trade negotiations (see Trump’s New Coercive Toolkit).The proposed tariffs, released by the Office of the United States Trade Representative after an eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity,” are designed to be more legally robust than President Donald Trump’s invalidated reciprocal tariff regime. China remains the principal target, followed by Vietnam, India and other Asian emerging economies. Washington intends to respect tariff ceilings negotiated under bilateral trade agreements, meaning that the European Union’s tariff will be capped at 15% (USTR kept the option to raise it to 20%). That should avert a renewed tariff war between two of the world’s three largest trading powers.
